PERSONAL LIABILITY OF OWNERS, OFFICERS, AND MANAGERS FOR A BUSINESS’S UNPAID SALES, PAYROLL, AND FEDERAL TRUST FUND TAXES (REV. & TAX. CODE § 6829; UNEMP. INS. CODE § 1735; 26 U.S.C. §§ 6671–6672; STATE BD. OF EQUALIZATION V. WIRICK; CAVANAGH V. CALIFORNIA UNEMPLOYMENT INS. APPEALS BD.) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme Retail, LLC

PURPOSE AND SCOPE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet, prepared by Jane Doe, states what California and federal law provide about when an individual — an officer, director, member, manager, partner, or major stockholder — becomes personally liable, by statute, for taxes that a business entity collected from customers or withheld from employees and then failed to pay over. The subject is not the equitable alter ego doctrine, under which a court disregards the entity because it was never respected as a separate thing, and it is not the liability a buyer of a business assumes by failing to withhold from the purchase price. It is the separate, statutory route by which the taxing agencies reach the people who ran the business: California Revenue and Taxation Code section 6829 for unpaid sales and use tax, California Unemployment Insurance Code section 1735 for unpaid employer contributions and employee withholdings, and 26 United States Code sections 6671 and 6672 for the federal trust fund recovery penalty. The sheet reproduces the statutory text, sets out what the two published California Court of Appeal decisions construing these sections say — State Board of Equalization v. Wirick (2001) 93 Cal.App.4th 411 and Cavanagh v. California Unemployment Insurance Appeals Board (2004) 118 Cal.App.4th 83 — and records where the published authority runs out. Where a business name appears below, that is Acme Retail, LLC; the sheet can also be read on its own, without any name filled in, as a general reference to what these authorities say. It states the law. It does not evaluate whether any person is a responsible person, whether any failure to pay was willful, whether any assessment is timely, or what any agency or court would decide.

SALES AND USE TAX: WHO SECTION 6829 REACHES, AND THE EVENT THAT TRIGGERS IT
California Revenue and Taxation Code section 6829 makes named individuals personally liable for a business entity’s unpaid sales and use tax. Three features of subdivision (a) define its reach. First, the trigger is an event in the life of the entity: the liability arises “upon the termination, dissolution, or abandonment” of the business of a corporation, partnership, limited partnership, limited liability partnership, or limited liability company. Second, the class of persons reached is defined by function rather than by title: any officer, member, manager, partner, or other person having control or supervision of, or charged with responsibility for, the filing of returns or the payment of tax, or who is under a duty to act for the entity in complying with the Sales and Use Tax Law. Third, the statute states that this liability attaches “notwithstanding any provision in the Corporations Code to the contrary” — that is, the limited-liability provisions of the entity statutes do not by their own force displace it. The liability runs to the unpaid taxes and to interest and penalties on those taxes, and it attaches only if the person willfully fails to pay or to cause to be paid taxes due from the entity.

TWO STATUTORY LIMITS ON SECTION 6829 LIABILITY: THE PERIOD OF CONTROL, AND PROOF THAT TAX REIMBURSEMENT WAS CHARGED
Section 6829 contains two express limits that narrow the rule of subdivision (a). Subdivision (b) confines the amount: the officer, member, manager, partner, or other person is liable only for taxes that became due during the period that person had the control, supervision, responsibility, or duty to act described in subdivision (a), plus interest and penalties on those taxes. Subdivision (c) adds a precondition of proof: personal liability may be imposed only if the department can establish that the entity included or added tax reimbursement in or to the selling price of tangible personal property sold in the conduct of its business, or that the entity consumed tangible personal property and failed to pay the tax to the seller, or included use tax on the billing and collected it, or issued a receipt for the use tax and failed to report and pay it. Both subdivisions were amended by Stats. 2024, ch. 499, § 15 (SB 1528): subdivision (b) was changed from “he or she had” to “they had,” and subdivision (c) from “the board” to “the department,” reflecting the transfer of sales and use tax administration from the State Board of Equalization to the California Department of Tax and Fee Administration.

WHAT “WILLFULLY FAILS TO PAY OR TO CAUSE TO BE PAID” MEANS IN SECTION 6829
Section 6829 does not leave willfulness to judicial construction. Subdivision (d) supplies a definition for purposes of the section: “willfully fails to pay or to cause to be paid” means that the failure was the result of an intentional, conscious, and voluntary course of action. The definition speaks to the character of the course of action, not to motive, and the statute’s text does not require a showing of bad faith, an intent to defraud, or knowledge that the conduct was unlawful. The 2024 amendment made one change to this subdivision: it inserted a comma after “this section,” so that the current text reads “For purposes of this section, ‘willfully fails…’” where the pre-2024 text read “For purposes of this section ‘willfully fails…’” The defining words themselves were not changed.

HOW THE LIABILITY IS COLLECTED, AND THE OUTER DEADLINE FOR SERVING A NOTICE OF DEFICIENCY DETERMINATION
Subdivision (e) of section 6829 provides that, except as provided in subdivision (f), the sum due under the section may be collected by determination and collection in the manner provided in chapter 5 (commencing with section 6451) and chapter 6 (commencing with section 6701) of the Sales and Use Tax Law — that is, through the same deficiency-determination and collection machinery the agency uses against the business itself, rather than by an original lawsuit on a common law theory. Subdivision (f) supplies the outer time limit for the first step. A notice of deficiency determination under the section must be served within three years after the last day of the calendar month following the quarterly period in which the department obtains actual knowledge — through its audit or compliance activities, or by written communication from the business or its representative — of the termination, dissolution, or abandonment of the business, or within eight years after the last day of the calendar month following the quarterly period in which the business was terminated, dissolved, or abandoned, whichever period expires earlier. Subdivision (f) also states that a filing of a notice of termination, dissolution, or abandonment with a state or local agency other than the department does not constitute actual knowledge by the department.

CASE LAW: SECTION 6829 REACHES FORMER OFFICERS, NOT ONLY THOSE IN CHARGE WHEN THE BUSINESS CEASES
In State Board of Equalization v. Wirick (2001) 93 Cal.App.4th 411, the Third District Court of Appeal decided whether section 6829 reaches a responsible officer who had already resigned before the corporation ceased business. Wirick had been the chief financial officer of a corporation that added sales tax reimbursement to its sales prices and failed to pay the tax over; he resigned roughly one year before the corporation was terminated, abandoned, or dissolved, and he argued that the statute’s present-tense description of responsible persons limited liability to those in charge at the moment the corporation ceased. The court rejected that reading. Because the Legislature has directed, in the Revenue and Taxation Code, that the present tense includes the past tense, the court held that section 6829 covers former officers as well as those in charge when the corporation ceases, and that subdivision (a), construed in accordance with that directive, provides for the personal liability of any responsible officer for unpaid sales tax upon termination, dissolution, or abandonment of the corporation. The judgment against Wirick for $431,894.20 in sales tax, interest, and penalties was affirmed.

CASE LAW: WHICH LIMITATION PERIODS APPLY TO A SECTION 6829 ASSESSMENT
Wirick also addressed the argument that reading section 6829 to reach former officers would let the agency go back in time without limit. The court disagreed, reasoning from subdivision (e): because that subdivision makes the determination and collection machinery of chapters 5 and 6 of the Sales and Use Tax Law applicable to the section 6829 liability, the limitation periods in those chapters apply as well. The court stated that those chapters provide limitation periods for both a notice of deficiency and a suit to collect tax, identified section 6487 as supplying a three-year period (or eight years where no return was filed) for sending a notice of deficiency determination, noted that taxes become delinquent 30 days after the deficiency notice or 30 days after the order on a petition for redetermination, and stated that under section 6711 the Board may bring suit within three years after the delinquency of any tax. Answering the contention that section 6487 speaks only of a “taxpayer” and that a former officer is not one, the court said these provisions are made applicable to the officer by subdivision (e) of section 6829. The court also recorded that Wirick did not raise a statute of limitations defense in his case, so the application of these periods to particular facts was not decided.

CASE LAW: THE CONSTITUTIONAL VAGUENESS CHALLENGE TO SECTION 6829 WAS REJECTED
Wirick separately contended that reading section 6829 to reach former officers would render the statute unconstitutionally vague, because it would not give fair notice that a person could be personally liable for a corporation’s unpaid taxes after leaving the corporation. The Court of Appeal applied the civil-statute standard — a statute is upheld if it gives fair notice of the practice to be avoided and provides reasonably adequate standards to guide enforcement, with certainty requirements less exacting than for a criminal statute — and held that section 6829 easily meets it. The court stated that the reasonable and practical construction of the statute’s language, in light of the Revenue and Taxation Code’s present-tense directive, is that upon termination of a corporation any current or former officer may be personally liable for unpaid sales taxes of the corporation if the officer willfully failed to pay such taxes. As applied to the facts before it, the court observed that the officer had notice he could avoid personal liability by seeing that the taxes were paid when due, that he knew unpaid sales taxes were due when he left, and that his bargaining for indemnification indicated notice of potential liability.

A BOUNDARY: RESPONSIBLE-PERSON LIABILITY IS NOT THE SAME AS A BUYER’S WITHHOLDING LIABILITY, AND THE REMEDIES ARE CUMULATIVE
Two different provisions of the Sales and Use Tax Law impose personal liability on someone other than the selling business, and they run against different people. Section 6829, the subject of this document, runs against the people who ran the business — officers, members, managers, partners, and others with control or responsibility — when the business is terminated, dissolved, or abandoned. A separate provision runs against a purchaser: surveying the collection tools available to the agency, the court in Wirick listed, among them, the power to hold a purchaser of a business or stock of goods personally liable for unpaid tax if the purchaser failed to properly withhold from the purchase price to cover the tax liability, citing section 6812. The court noted, citing section 6827, that these remedies are cumulative. The same survey listed the agency’s powers to require security (section 6701), levy property (section 6703), impose a tax lien (section 6756), issue a warrant for collection (section 6776), and seize and sell personal property (section 6796), and recorded that no legal proceeding may be instituted to enjoin the collection of sales tax (section 6931), so that a retailer contesting liability must file a return, pay the tax, and seek a refund (sections 6901–6906).

PAYROLL TAXES: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE CODE SECTION 1735 AND WHO IT REACHES
California Unemployment Insurance Code section 1735 is the payroll-tax counterpart to Revenue and Taxation Code section 6829, and it is built differently. It makes any officer, major stockholder, or other person having charge of the affairs of a corporate, association, registered or foreign limited liability partnership, or limited liability company employing unit personally liable for the amount of contributions, withholdings, penalties, and interest due and unpaid by that employing unit, where the person willfully fails to pay contributions required by division 1 of the code or withholdings required by division 6 (commencing with section 13000) on the date on which they become delinquent. The section authorizes the Director of Employment Development to assess that officer, stockholder, or other person for the amount owed, applies the assessment and petition provisions of article 8 (commencing with section 1126) and article 9 (commencing with section 1176) of chapter 4 of part 1 and sections 1221 through 1224 to such assessments, and gives the director all of the collection remedies set out in chapter 7. THE FEDERAL COUNTERPART: THE TRUST FUND RECOVERY PENALTY OF 26 U.S.C. SECTION 6672 AND WHO COUNTS AS A “PERSON”
Federal law imposes a parallel personal liability, and its structure differs again from both California statutes. Under 26 United States Code section 6672(a), any person required to collect, truthfully account for, and pay over any tax imposed by title 26 who willfully fails to collect the tax, or to truthfully account for and pay it over, or who willfully attempts in any manner to evade or defeat the tax or its payment, is liable — in addition to other penalties provided by law — to a penalty equal to the total amount of the tax evaded, or not collected, or not accounted for and paid over. The person reached is defined by 26 United States Code section 6671(b), which provides that for purposes of the subchapter the term “person” includes an officer or employee of a corporation, or a member or employee of a partnership, who as such officer, employee, or member is under a duty to perform the act in respect of which the violation occurs. Section 6671(a) provides that penalties under the subchapter are paid on notice and demand and are assessed and collected in the same manner as taxes. The federal provision is not conditioned on the termination, dissolution, or abandonment of the business, and it measures the penalty by the full amount of the tax rather than by the tax attributable to any particular period of control.

California Revenue and Taxation Code section 6829 makes named individuals personally liable for a business entity’s unpaid sales and use tax. Three features of subdivision (a) define its reach. First, the trigger is an event in the life of the entity: the liability arises “upon the termination, dissolution, or abandonment” of the business of a corporation, partnership, limited partnership, limited liability partnership, or limited liability company. Second, the class of persons reached is defined by function rather than by title: any officer, member, manager, partner, or other person having control or supervision of, or charged with responsibility for, the filing of returns or the payment of tax, or who is under a duty to act for the entity in complying with the Sales and Use Tax Law. Third, the statute states that this liability attaches “notwithstanding any provision in the Corporations Code to the contrary” — that is, the limited-liability provisions of the entity statutes do not by their own force displace it. The liability runs to the unpaid taxes and to interest and penalties on those taxes, and it attaches only if the person willfully fails to pay or to cause to be paid taxes due from the entity.

expectedJSON.body: In State Board of Equalization v. Wirick (2001) 93 Cal.App.4th 411, the Third District Court of Appeal decided whether section 6829 reaches a responsible officer who had already resigned before the corporation ceased business. Wirick had been the chief financial officer of a corporation that added sales tax reimbursement to its sales prices and failed to pay the tax over; he resigned roughly one year before the corporation was terminated, abandoned, or dissolved, and he argued that the statute’s present-tense description of responsible persons limited liability to those in charge at the moment the corporation ceased. The court rejected that reading. Because the Legislature has directed, in the Revenue and Taxation Code, that the present tense includes the past tense, the court held that section 6829 covers former officers as well as those in charge when the corporation ceases, and that subdivision (a), construed in accordance with that directive, provides for the personal liability of any responsible officer for unpaid sales tax upon termination, dissolution, or abandonment of the corporation. The judgment against Wirick for $431,894.20 in sales tax, interest, and penalties was affirmed.

The officer there argued that if the Legislature had meant to reach former officers under Revenue and Taxation Code section 6829, it would have followed the model of Unemployment Insurance Code section 1735. California Unemployment Insurance Appeals Board (2004) 118 Cal.App.4th 83 arose from Employment Development Department assessments issued against an individual under Unemployment Insurance Code section 1735 for unpaid unemployment insurance contributions and other tax liabilities of his insolvent landscaping business. expectedJSON.body: Federal law imposes a parallel personal liability, and its structure differs again from both California statutes. Under 26 United States Code section 6672(a), any person required to collect, truthfully account for, and pay over any tax imposed by title 26 who willfully fails to collect the tax, or to truthfully account for and pay it over, or who willfully attempts in any manner to evade or defeat the tax or its payment, is liable — in addition to other penalties provided by law — to a penalty equal to the total amount of the tax evaded, or not collected, or not accounted for and paid over. The person reached is defined by 26 United States Code section 6671(b), which provides that for purposes of the subchapter the term “person” includes an officer or employee of a corporation, or a member or employee of a partnership, who as such officer, employee, or member is under a duty to perform the act in respect of which the violation occurs. Section 6671(a) provides that penalties under the subchapter are paid on notice and demand and are assessed and collected in the same manner as taxes. The federal provision is not conditioned on the termination, dissolution, or abandonment of the business, and it measures the penalty by the full amount of the tax rather than by the tax attributable to any particular period of control.
